title: Raga Jaitsri
hook: Jaitsri opens with a hand placed on a forehead

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Dhanasri, a whole sequence of aartis from the sky to a farmhouse kitchen, and your line was the sky's aarti. Did you look up long enough to see the lamps? Day one thousand eighty-six.

Nothing gets fixed when someone slips into a dark room at three in the morning, sits on the edge of a feverish child's bed, and lays a cool hand on the child's forehead. The fever is still there. But the room changes. That kind of strength doesn't shout. It arrives, it stays, and it steadies. Today's raga opens its pages with a hand like that. Today: Raga Jaitsri, a raga that tradition links with longing and quiet strength.
screen: `A FEVER AT THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `A COOL HAND ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `STRENGTH THAT DOESN'T SHOUT.`

segments.voice: Jaitsri comes after Dhanasri in the Granth's order. Its first hymn is by Guru Ram Das, mahala four, and it begins with two pictures. In paraphrase: the jewel of the Name has come to dwell in my heart; the Guru has placed his hand on my forehead. Hold those two together. The jewel is inside, hidden, precious, not for show. The hand is on the outside, a familiar gesture of blessing: an elder's palm resting on a younger head. In the hymn the two belong together: a touch from outside, a treasure within. Now the longing. A raga that tradition links with longing usually sounds like reaching for something far away. But this hymn starts from what has already been given. The longing in it is the longing to stay near the one who gave it, to keep feeling that hand. Strength and longing turn out to be the same movement, seen from two sides: you lean toward what steadies you. Notice too what the hymn doesn't claim. It doesn't say the hard things vanished. It says something precious now lives inside, put there by a touch. That is quiet strength. Not the strength of a wall, which keeps everything out, but the strength of a keel under a boat, which you never see and which keeps it upright in the wind. Jaitsri's opening pages are calm, and the calm has weight. Today's line: quiet strength.
screen: `JAITSRI FOLLOWS DHANASRI.` · `THE JEWEL OF THE NAME IN THE HEART.` · `A HAND PLACED ON THE FOREHEAD.` · `A KEEL, NOT A WALL.` · then, large: `QUIET STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Jaitsri, and receive a steadying hand. If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Jaitsri first. Then sit, and if it feels right, rest your own palm lightly on your forehead for a few breaths. Feel its weight and warmth. Then let the hand fall to your lap, and see whether the steadiness stays. Bring to mind someone whose presence has steadied you without a word. Stay with them a while. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly as you think of them. If you don't, simply let them be remembered. The bell holds the time.
Raga Jaitsri. The raga after Dhanasri, linked by tradition with longing and quiet strength, which opens with the jewel of the Name in the heart and the Guru's hand on the forehead. Today's word.
Your line: quiet strength. Today, steady someone without fixing anything: sit with them, stay a little longer, say less. Day one thousand eighty-six.

howItsDone: Shabads from the Jaitsri section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Jaitsri in kirtan, and Guru Ram Das's opening hymn, about the jewel of the Name and the Guru's hand on the forehead, is one of them.
